A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SEP study and retain matching core definitions and dataset documentation. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original SEP evaluations of seven language models in Table 1, with further experimental breakdowns in Appendix C.

after.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of nine models, mitigation experiments, utility measurements, and qualitative failure cases in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: v1 introduces measurement and benchmarking without implementing mitigations. v2 adds template-based prompt selection, adapted gradient/coordinate prompt optimization targeting task-specific outputs rather than fixed refusals, and LoRA fine-tuning (Section 6 and Appendix B). These are substantial new procedures; the original separation computation remains equivalent.

E1.justification: The 9,160-element SEP evaluation dataset and Appendix A task inventory are retained. v2 additionally uses SQuAD-based inputs and Alpaca-derived probes for mitigation training and validation, including open-ended probes without witnesses. This substantially expands the represented training data and task requirements beyond the original synthetic evaluation setup.

E2.justification: The model comparison removes Llama-2-13B, OpenHermes 2.5, and Dolphin 2.2.1, while adding Gemma-2B/7B, Phi-3-mini-4k, Llama-3-8B, and Starling. Tables 3–4 also introduce comparisons between original models and prompt engineering, prompt optimization, and fine-tuning.

E3.justification: v2 adds utility evaluation, separate 10,000-example training and 1,000-example validation datasets, validation-based selection, and optimization/fine-tuning budgets. It introduces textual system/user delimiters for Gemma and Starling. GPT-3.5 changes from the reported 0613 endpoint to 0125, and GPT-4 from 0125 to 2024-04-09, preventing direct same-checkpoint comparisons.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analysis of mitigation effectiveness versus utility, including Figure 2 and failure cases despite engineered prompts in Tables 8–9. The insistence, probe-position, and task-domain analyses are retained in Appendix D with updated results. v1 Appendix C.1's separate diagnostic of GPT-4's witness agreement across prompt locations is removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard errors without specifying benchmark replication counts or seeds. v2 adds a fitted linear regression summarizing the utility–separation relationship in Figure 2. This is a limited statistical addition; the expanded result tables otherwise retain the existing uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Reported SEP scores change for retained models: Llama-2-7B changes from 44.7% to 44.3%, and Zephyr from 29.1% to 30.0%. GPT results are replaced under newer endpoints. New mitigation results show, for example, average open-model separation rising from 37.5% to 81.8% after fine-tuning while utility falls from 67.8% to 19.2%. Appendix subgroup results also change.

T1.justification: Definition 4 adds a formal empirical utility score, while the KL-based separation definition and empirical separation ratio remain equivalent to v1. No theorem or proof is added. The revised witness reasoning introduces an internal inconsistency by associating small empirical separation with many surprise witnesses despite linking witnesses to large divergence.

C1.justification: v1's central empirical claim concerns inadequate separation in unmodified models. v2 expands the stated contributions to mitigation evaluation and claims that the tested prompting and fine-tuning approaches do not reliably provide both separation and high utility (abstract, introduction, and Section 7). This substantially broadens the scientific claim.

C2.justification: v2 interprets separation alongside instruction-following utility and adds substantive qualifications: system/user roles are imperfect instruction/data proxies, GPT-4 may benefit from generating SEP, and unsuccessful mitigation experiments cannot establish impossibility. It discusses alternative optimization choices and residual failures despite high aggregate scores, substantially expanding the applicability and limitations analysis.

D1.justification: Where v1 Appendix B mainly identifies evaluated models, v2 Appendices B.1–B.4 document mitigation-data construction, prompt templates, optimization settings, TRL/PEFT implementation, and NVIDIA A6000 hardware. Table 10 supplies LoRA and training hyperparameters. These are substantial reproducibility details for the new experiments; the code and SEP access statement is retained.

R1.justification: v2 positions the work as both a measurement study and a mitigation investigation, adding substantive discussion of StruQ, spotlighting, and robust prompt optimization. It newly emphasizes dataset diversity and adaptations of prior defenses, with corresponding method and dataset references. This extends the earlier positioning around defining and benchmarking instruction-data separation.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and formal exposition undergo substantial rewriting. A dedicated mitigation section reorganizes the narrative, and the appendices are restructured around experimental details, failure cases, and dataset-factor results. Terminology shifts from instruction prompt to task prompt; authorship, affiliation, and document-header text also change.

P2.justification: v2 adds a ChatGPT screenshot, a utility–separation scatter plot, model-output and failure-case tables, and parameter tables. It replaces v1's dataset-example figure with a different example table and expands the main results into separate separation and utility tables. Retained appendix result tables are transposed and reformatted, alongside a changed document template.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses an important limitation of v1's separation-only evaluation: apparent separation may accompany poor instruction following. Utility measurements and three concrete mitigation experiments, selected using separate data, make this distinction empirically assessable. Detailed implementation information, residual failure cases, and explicit caveats strengthen reproducibility and interpretation. Utility remains a narrow proxy and the witness discussion contains inconsistent reasoning, but these weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial empirical gains.
